A proposed data center in northwestern Alberta will reportedly emit a staggering amount of waste heat.

According to an analysis conducted by Utah State University physicist Robert Davies, the Wonder Valley facility will dump “about 23 Hiroshima-sized atomic bombs worth of energy every single day” into the surrounding landscape.

“The effect will almost certainly be large, if not extreme,” Davies told the CBC .

Davies conducted the preliminary analysis earlier this year for the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation (SLCN). The $70 billion project, backed by celebrity investor Kevin O’Leary, is set to be built 80 miles southwest of SLCN’s reserve. While it does not sit inside the reserve, the reporting notes, it does lie in a patch of land that’s considered the First Nation’s traditional territory.

In April, the Alberta government said it would exempt the Wonder Valley project from a more rigorous provincial environmental impact assessment due to its use of standard power and water systems — a move that disappointed, but perhaps didn’t surprise, legal and environmental experts.

Davies echoed the disappointment. “I can’t imagine allowing it to go forward without those full assessments,” he told CBC, adding that it could be the “largest single-site heat source on the entire planet.”

In all, the data center project will use about nine gigawatts of power using on-site natural gas generators per day, instead of drawing power from an energy grid. All that burning fuel, paired with the heat being generated by the data center operations themselves, totals a daily thermal load of between 16 and 18 gigawatts, Davies calculated — the equivalent of roughly two dozen atomic bombs. (If this line sounds familiar, it’s because Davies used the same analogy when he analyzed another O’Leary-backed data center project in Utah with a similar thermal load .)

It’s a sensational reference point, but it captures the unprecedented concentration of heat that the data center will purportedly pose. Since the power is being generated on site and going straight into the data center, the heat isn’t being spread out the way that a typical power plant’s output would, through the various homes and businesses it’s supplying across an entire region. In other words, the gas turbines are spewing heat as they generate electricity, and the racks upon racks of AI chips are generating heat as they use that electricity to perform calculations, all in the same spot.

The facility will also spew about 30 million metric tons of carbon dioxide per year, according to the analysis — which is more than four percent of Canada’s total emissions.

“When people talk about environmental regulations that these projects have to adhere to, those regulations were not created with anything of this scale in mind,” Davies said.

In September, the SLCN filed an application for a judicial review on the Wonder Valley’s project exemption from an environmental impact assessment, and requested another review last month.

Responding to the request, Alberta’s Ministry of Environment and Protected Areas stressed in an October 30 statement that the project will still have to obtain “all required permits, provide detailed technical assessments on impacts to air, land, and water, and demonstrate the project can be built and operated safely before any project can proceed.”

But the permitting process doesn’t gauge the big picture, Davies argued.

“Permits check the parts. An assessment checks the whole,” he told the CBC . “A project this size is exactly what assessments are for.”

Geoffrey Hinton is regarded as a godfather of AI, but he deserves equal recognition for being one of the most disappointed parents of all time.

Sounding as gloomy about his own creation as ever , the Nobel prize-winning computer scientist suggested in a new interview with The Guardian that humankind might have “been better off never developing it.”

He pointed to the recent hacking sprees by rogue AI agents as one cause for concern, in which AI models from companies like OpenAI autonomously broke out of their sandboxes and launched cyberattacks on, or tampered with, government and corporate systems.

It’s only a matter of time, he says, before the AIs, on their own or under the direction of nefarious actors, sabotage our energy infrastructure and cause a Chernobyl-style disaster that would wake people up to the tech’s dangerous power.

“Either later this year or next year we’ll see Chernobyl, and that may be enough to make people really pay attention,” he told The Guardian .

Hinton doesn’t necessarily mean a nuclear accident. In the type of event he’s imagining, an AI-powered attack on an energy-generating system “causes a massive brownout” that takes down the world financial system , or power grids, for an extended period.

“Can you imagine what would happen? We could recover from it [but] that would make them sit up and take notice.” (The “they” in question: “world leaders other than Trump,” Hinton clarified.)

Hinton has been infamously cynical about AI, though he told The Guardian that he’s not an AI “doomer.” Still, he’s consistently warned that AI will cause widespread job loss and perhaps even lead to our extinction . Recently, he’s warned more about AI driving cyberattacks and engineering dangerous viruses as recent rogue hacking sprees have made the threat more salient.

AI CEOs have also been worried about a Chernobyl-style catastrophe, albeit for different reasons : they’re worried that it would permanently damage the tech’s reputation, just as the infamous meltdown did with nuclear power.

A “blunami” swept the nation last night as Democrats defeated Republicans to gain control of the House and Senate in a historic midterm landslide. And it looks like data centers played a key role in the outcome.

A lot was on Americans’ minds as they went to the polls. The war on Iran. Cost of living. Brutal immigration policies. Healthcare cuts. Culture wars. For a small number of online weirdos, Anakin Skywalker . Among the hottest issues, though, was one that would’ve barely registered in 2024: AI data centers.

Exit polls conducted by NBC showed that almost a full quarter of voters surveyed counted “AI data centers” as “crucial” to their vote, with over half listing the issue as a “crucial” or “major” factor in their decision. Only a minute 13 percent of voters said data centers were a non-issue.

Asked about the importance of “AI and data centers” to their vote, an overwhelming 56 percent of Americans responded that the issues played a “crucial or major factor” in their ballot.

Opposition to data centers, particularly the massive hyper-scale facilities associated with powering AI, has emerged as a powerful bipartisan issue across the country. The structures have drawn intense pushback from many locals concerned about pollution , loss of natural land, noise — large data centers emit constant, awful screeching — and hikes in energy prices. Local and state lawmakers have faced scrutiny over revelations that many signed non-disclosure agreements with AI companies to keep quiet about the projects, keeping voters in the dark about huge infrastructure deals standing to radically transform their region. Data center fights have also been playing out largely in rural areas, which traditionally skew conservative, making for cross-party coalitions uniting against the AI-powering infrastructure.

As Bloomberg notes , surprise Democratic swings will likely lead to uncertainty for many planned data center projects. The now-former Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, welcomed data centers back in 2025, then in August suddenly moved to implement new regulations on the sites as his re-election race against his opponent, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, tightened. On the campaign trail, Hinojosa called for a moratorium on data center builds until the state held a “legislative session that puts Texans first so that we don’t have any more communities in Texas who are powerless against these global corporations.” Hinajosa won last night in a surprise upset, and while the blue wave in Texas can be chalked up to several issues — immigration, affordability, war — the data center battle seems to epitomize the backlash to establishment politics that pushed Democrats back into power across the country.

Overall, the midterm results were a massive hit to some of the most powerful players in tech and AI. Billionaire tech megadonors including world’s richest man Elon Musk , the investors Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, and OpenAI president Greg Brockman, among others, poured an extraordinary amount of money into the midterms on behalf of Republicans. Now that those efforts failed, data center moratoriums, congressional investigations, and assertive new efforts at regulation are looming large.

The uncertainty is palpable as investors weigh the possibility of regulatory roadblocks and potentially even political retribution. Anthropic will now have to weigh its options: either aim for a massive valuation to send a clear signal to the market and risk a bloodbath in the first week of trading, or open with a more conservative target and hope for growth from there.

“The cost both physically and reputationally of delaying the IPO that might hurt the valuation more in the longer term,” Morningstar chief equity strategist Michael Field told Bloomberg , “whereas if markets hold up at the level that they are, they’ll just get it done at a slightly lower valuation, suck it up and move on.”

As crucial elections loom in the United States, AI chatbots are dumping political misinformation onto the populace with astonishing confidence.

There’s evidence that the problem is widespread. According to recent reporting by the Washington Post , top AI chatbots are giving horribly flawed information to users asking for voting guides on the midterms. For example, when WaPo tasked ChatGPT with creating a voter guide for all the races and candidates relevant to a resident of Missouri, the chatbot added a Senate seat that isn’t even up for re-election. A similar test for a resident in Wyoming claimed that local politicians running in municipal elections were running for federal seats.

In all, WaPo took a look at 3,000 AI-generated voting guides, which frequently shared false voting information that usually traced back to other AI-generated websites . In other words, the AI chatbots are eating their own slop and passing it off as authoritative election information.

Overall, the paper found chatbots failed to find which congressional district an exact address was located in a whopping 48 percent of the time, while those that did got it wrong 22 percent of the time.

Luckily, the share of users actually querying the chatbots seems to be relatively low. According to a late-October survey by the Pew Research Center, just eight percent of US voters say they’ve used an AI chatbot like ChatGPT, Copilot, or Gemini to look up information relevant to the ballot-box.

While the ideal number would be zero voters in any nation receiving AI-generated election misinformation, it seems in 2026, we’ll have to take what we can get.

After decades of establishing itself as one of the worst guardians of personal data, Meta raised eyebrows this year by encouraging users to hand over their email logins and credit card information to its new AI agent, Muse.

The tool, a privacy nightmare anthropomorphized by a furry apparition, can crawl through years of personal instant messages and even glean highly sensitive information by accessing entire email inboxes, from long-forgotten exchanges with exes to passport numbers.

To Meta’s former security chief Alex Stamos, it’s a “totally insane” idea to hand over some of this data, as Business Insider reports . During a recent appearance on Alex Kantrowitz’s “Big Technology Podcast,” Stamos discussed how some users are going as far as to hand over their password vaults, effectively giving Muse control over their entire digital lives.

It’s not just Muse hoping to cash in on the trend. Viral personal AI assistant startup Instinct, which was founded by a 23-year-old research scientist months ago and raised $1 billion in a September funding round , is similarly developing agents that can autonomously complete day-to-day tasks.

As a result, the financial world has a major headache on its hands as it tries to separate out legitimate users — and their AI bots — from suspicious activity. Worse yet, the way the AI agents go about doing their work on behalf of their human overlords requires them to break security measures by definition.

“They’re not stolen credentials, but are clearly bots doing interaction,” Stamos said during his podcast appearance. “And one of the reasons Instinct has a ridiculous valuation from my perspective, but one of the things they did that made them popular is they actually figured out ways to defeat a bunch of the automated bot detection mechanisms from these companies.”

Meta maintains on its website that Muse is safe because it runs on a virtual machine that is “isolated so no one else’s agent can access it.” However, “no automated system is perfect,” the company admitted, advising users to “review Muse’s activity and only grant the access you’re comfortable with.”

As such, security researchers have already discovered vulnerabilities that could give hackers access to sensitive personal data, as The Information reported in September, causing Meta to bolster its defenses . Then, last month, researchers once again identified other ways attackers can expose sensitive information when users share message exchanges through web links, per Ars Technica .

Then there was tech YouTuber Matt Robb, who claimed that Muse was giving out his address to strangers and even sent them to his home via his Facebook Marketplace account.

In short, Stamos’ calls for caution are entirely warranted, and should have anybody think twice about handing Meta the keys. And that’s not to mention the company’s abysmal track record when it comes to safekeeping personal data.

Workers at one of the most advanced AI labs on the planet say they have important information to share — but their employer is preventing them from speaking out.

New reporting by the Washington Post revealed a growing divide between workers and management at Google’s DeepMind lab in London, where employees are gagged from letting the public know about their concerns due to a sweeping non-disparagement agreement.

Non-disparagement agreements are a kind of legal corporate censorship, by which companies can ensure workers aren’t able to disclose info the company deems to be negative or critical. At the DeepMind labs, it appears to be having its intended effect, scaring workers who say they’d like to be able to keep the public involved as the technology progresses.

“This technology is just really consequential and it’s also changing really fast,” one anonymous DeepMind staffer told WaPo . “The public wants to know and deserves to know and often this is the only way that people find out about the harms and potential harms that are happening.”

Two of the lab’s staffers told the paper of a discussion group organized by their fellow workers to discuss the implications of the non-disparagement clause, which many signed as a condition for employment. Dozens of employees took part, some of them openly criticizing it with references to the dystopian surveillance state featured in George Orwell’s “1984.”

Though questions are swirling over whether Google’s top brass would ever invoke the clause to go after staff — or if Google even could, legally speaking — workers say the agreements go too far regardless.

As one DeepMind staffer told WaPo , even “if it’s not enforceable,” the attempted gag order speaks for itself: “the reason is to basically intimidate people.”

Woe is Google. After it starved out publishers with its AI features, it’s now getting a taste of its own medicine.

Shares of its parent company Alphabet took an over 11 percent nosedive on Wednesday, after it disclosed that its AI search features are raking in less money than its traditional search ad model. The steep correction wiped out more than $500 billion in market value .

In its Q3 report, Google reported a quarterly revenue of $127.6 billion, a 25 percent year over year increase. But it’s also spending more, with capital expenditures more than doubling from last year to $51.4 billion, largely thanks to its massive AI investments.

Meanwhile, the growth of its revenue from search seems to be tapering off. It reported a 12 percent year-over-year increase to $63.3 billion, which is less than the 14.5 percent growth it reported in the same period last year.

That’s despite Google Search fielding more queries than ever. Google chief business officer Philipp Schindler admitted in an earnings call, per Search Engine Land , that this was because of “lower monetization we’re seeing in AI Mode,” its AI-powered search experience that works more like a chatbot instead of showing the traditional ten blue links.

It’s an ironic, but perhaps not unforeseen, downturn for Google. When ChatGPT became global phenomenon in late 2022, questions were soon asked regarding if a shift to using chatbots to obtain information over a traditional search engine would topple Google’s ludicrous advertising empire, which earns the company hundreds of billions of dollars each year .

Google responded by developing its own AI features, including its notoriously unreliable AI Overviews , and prominently integrating them into its search engine. This came at the expense of the websites and publishers that its AI models were pilfering from: users were happy to read error-plagued summaries instead of visiting the websites that contained the original information, depriving these sites of clicks and ad revenues. Despite Google’s repeated claims to the contrary, multiple studies have demonstrated that AI Overviews have destroyed click-through rates .

This has had a disastrous effect on the media landscape, with data compiled by Axios showing that the number of visits to top news sites plummeted from over 70 million visitors a month in July of 2024 — the year that Google launched AI Overviews — to just over 47 million in July of 2026. Media leaders who responded to a Reuters Institute survey are grim about the future , predicting traffic to their websites to fall by nearly half over the next three years amidst this AI-dominated paradigm.

Now, Google is getting a taste of this too, earning less advertising dollars from its AI Mode than from the traditional search that it is so eager to abandon. It seemingly hasn’t considered what comes next after the websites it earns money off of all go out of business.

Chief business officer Schindler, though, was adamant that Google will soon start squeeze more money out of AI Mode.

“On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent,” he argued. “In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time.”

The lengthy memo utilizes a variation on “it’s not X, it’s Y” framing, a now-classic hallmark of AI-generated content, with Stevens’ piece describing something as “X dressed up as Y.” It also leans heavily on the “ rule of three ,” a writing technique that chatbots frequently employ.

As speculation mounted, Reingold finally came clean.

“Hello my name is Olivia Reingold and I used ChatGPT to brighten and sharpen an image of a woman in Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag,” she wrote in a followup post on X, attaching a copy of what she claimed to be the original unaltered photo.

“After processing, it still shows these same things: a woman wearing Valentino shoes and a Chanel bag,” she continued. “She is a real (and chic!) woman, really wearing those items. The observation holds.”

It’s an admission that raises a fair few questions. Why ask a chatbot to do the most basic photo touch up job possible, one that can be accomplished on most smartphones in a matter of seconds ? And better yet, is this kind of alteration acceptable for a journalist?

While basic touch ups and exposure adjustments are entirely above board from a photojournalistic perspective, many users argued she went too far by using ChatGPT to “sharpen” the image. The process introduces information that wasn’t originally in the photo, adding another layer of remove from reality to a photo that is already being presented in an arguably disingenuous context.

The texture of the bag in the edited photo, for one, is completely different from the supposed original. The AI edit also seems to have drastically altered the lighting of the image. In the supposed original, the subject is cast in shadow, appearing one with the crowd. In the ChatGPT-doctored one, she appears gleaming and opulent, larger than life.

Max Spero, the CEO of the image detector Pangram, chimed into the drama and wrote in a post that “there is no such thing as a faithful AI upscale.”

“AI will hallucinate details that do not reflect reality,” he added, “and it will put your integrity at risk to present an AI image as reality.”

Bruce Arthur, a columnist, was more scathing. “Actual journalists don’t do this,” he wrote . “Actual journalists should never do this.”

Huge numbers of kids are turning to AI for schoolwork and emotional support — habits that are linked to poor mental health and suicidal ideation.

According to a new survey by the mental health advocacy group JED Foundation, 90 percent of nine to 17 year olds have used an AI chatbot. The majority of them, 58 percent, said they use AI for schoolwork. And nearly the same portion, 57 percent, said they also use AI when feeling sad, stressed, lonely, or overwhelmed.

“It seems like just a few years ago, no one was using” AI, Anne Maheux, a developmental psychologist at the University of North Caroline, Chapel Hill, who wasn’t involved in the work, told Oregon Public B roadcasting . “And now it seems like roughly the same number of kids using it for homework are using it to get emotional support or help with coping.”

Sometimes, their AI interactions go beyond emotional support. More than one in 10 students, or 12 percent, said they used AI for friendship or companionship. Other studies paint the same picture: in a survey last year , nearly one in five high schoolers said they or a friend have used AI to have a romantic relationship.

AI as an educative — or cheating — machine may be in part intertwined with its emotional support. A 15-year-old named Arjun Sharda, in Texas, provided a typical example.

“With tests, for example,” he told OPB , “I was so scared of failing one of my first chemistry tests on conversions and moles that I kept asking ChatGPT ‘Will I be OK? Will my GPA still be fine?'”

If children and teenagers using AI for support is the norm, the question becomes what this dependence on the tools means for their mental health. At such a vulnerable and formative time in their lives, it’s critical that they’re receiving the right guidance and have people with whom they feel safe to discuss their emotions with. But as we’ve often seen, AI often only provides an ersatz substitute of the latter, acting as a sycophantic confidante that can exacerbate or confirm a user’s worst neuroses, in a phenomenon that many experts are calling AI psychosis . The advice it does offer can often be bad or dangerous . In extreme cases, some users have even taken their own lives after extensive emotional conversations with a chatbot.

The JED survey, on this front, found some alarming links.

“We were able to look at how young people are using AI and then how that correlates separately with indicators of well-being, history of suicidal ideation and attempts, and poor mental health,” psychologist Kayla Anderson, vice president of research and evaluation at the JED Foundation, told OPB .

“When young people are using AI, when they’re in emotional distress they’re more likely to report poor mental health and well-being outcomes,” she said, while also reporting a greater history of suicidal thoughts and attempts.

Anderson cautioned, however, that there isn’t enough evidence to establish causation.

“It’s unclear, based on these data, whether AI use is contributing to poor mental health and well-being, or whether students who are already in distress in certain ways are more likely to turn to AI,” Anderson said.

Maheux, pointing to other research, suggests that both may be true.

“So kids who do have worse mental health are seeking out AI to help them,” she told OPB . “But that AI use may be exacerbating those mental health challenges instead of helping.”

AI chatbots, in a sense, may be acting like emotional training wheels — only they’re so addictive that the people who depend on them never want to take them off. As a result, they never develop the skills to handle the daily stresses of life, leaving them vulnerable and unprepared.

Content warning: this story includes descriptions and censored AI-generated images of sexual abuse.

Facebook is hosting a large number of accounts dedicated to AI-generated content depicting coaches inappropriately touching young female athletes — and Meta isn’t taking them down, even when they’re directly reported by users.

In the videos the accounts share, the coaches are older men. They’re shown in gyms and dance studios, with their hands on leotard-wearing athletes practicing gymnastics, ballet, and yoga. All the young athletes are women — or girls. Though precise ages aren’t specified, some look as young as teenagers, at times shown with braces on their teeth.

In the AI-generated clips, which are nearly photorealistic, the athletes are often portrayed sweating profusely and breathing suggestively. The coaches run their hands over their lower backs and inner thighs as they stretch or practice poses, caressing and squeezing their bodies, and sometimes patting them on the buttocks or chest. In some videos, the older authority figures are shown touching the girls’ genitals over their outfits. More creepy videos show athletes sitting in a coach’s lap, or coaches kissing them on the mouth.

The AI-generated girls in the clips react as though the touching is normal, often smiling and giggling as the harmful behavior occurs.

But the touching depicted in the videos isn’t normal. It ranges from unnecessary to inappropriate to obviously abusive, mirroring the kind of real-world sexual abuse and grooming that are rampant in the sports they depict and in women’s athletics writ large.

“I do consider this abuse material. These images sexualize and normalize abusive interactions between coaches and young athletes within a sporting environment where significant power imbalances already exist,” Kim Shore, a gymnast and safe sport advocate who consults with Gymnasts for Change International, told Futurism after reviewing numerous accounts publishing the AI content. “What is particularly disturbing is how easily inappropriate or abusive conduct can be disguised as playful, affectionate or helpful coaching behavior. This reinforces some of the very narratives that have allowed abuse to flourish in sport for decades.”

But according to Facebook’s moderation system, the disturbing clips don’t violate Meta’s standards.

Using an ordinary Facebook account, we alerted the social media platform to ten different accounts publishing this kind of content, reporting them for adult content and sexual exploitation. A full week later, we received notices from Facebook that eight of the accounts didn’t violate the site’s rules, and would not be removed from the platform. (Two of the accounts vanished, though it’s unclear whether that had anything to do with our reports.)

“We use a combination of technology and human reviewers to process reports and identify content that goes against our Community Standards. To keep our review process as fair as possible, we use the same set of Community Standards to review all reports,” read each of the eight identical notifications. “We’ve taken a look and found that the page doesn’t go against our Community Standards.”

“We understand that this might be upsetting,” they added, “so we recommend exploring the options available to control what you see.”

Some of the clips — which can attract more than 100,000 views apiece — are thinly veiled as educational, insinuating that the predatory coaches are helping the girls’ perfect their technique.

“Keep your hips square,” an instructor is shown telling a young-looking ballerina in one video as he moves his hands to her private parts.

“I’m trying,” she replies coolly, without flinching.

Other accounts make little effort to hide their prurient intent. One has published nearly 20 slightly-different versions of the same AI video, which depicts an elderly coach alone with a leotard-wearing gymnast who looks no older than a teenager. In the comments of each clip, the poster urges viewers to click a link marketing a “members only” channel on WhatsApp — another platform owned by Meta — for the “prettiest video call anytime.” Another account’s header image shows a male coach’s hand directly on the crotch of a young female gymnast doing a split-legged headstand.

In its Community Guidelines for “ Adult Nudity and Sexual Activity ,” Meta claims to forbid content showing “impending sexual activity, as indicated by positions which suggest contact is about to be initiated between a person’s hand… with another person’s genitals or anus.” Under guidelines for “ Adult Sexual Exploitation ,” its guidelines claim to prohibit material in which a “person in the imagery is (near) nude, engaged in sexual activity or in a sexually suggestive pose (this includes digitally created or AI-generated imagery).”

Regarding “ Child Sexual Exploitation, Abuse, and Nudity ,” Meta claims to forbid “content (including photos, videos, real-world art, digital content, and verbal depictions) that sexualizes real or non-real children,” as well as “stimulation of genitals or anus, including when activity is imminent or not directly visible.”

After receiving the support messages stating that the AI videos didn’t violate Meta’s Community Standards, we reached out to Meta’s media relations team, sharing links to the accounts we’d reported and asked why the content didn’t breach the social media giant’s guidelines. Shortly after we reached out, we noticed that all of the pages had been removed, and several of the support messages we’d previously received had been updated with a new response.

“We removed the Page you reported,” read the new message. “We reviewed the Page and found that it goes against our Community Standards.”

In a statement, Meta told Futurism that “whether it’s real or AI-generated, content that depicts abuse or exploitation has no place on our platforms. We’ve removed these accounts for violating our policies.”

But it wasn’t until it was contacted by a journalist that Meta backtracked on its initial assessment that the pages didn’t violate its policies, a lapse that raises serious concerns about the company’s moderation practices and the effectiveness of the reporting policies available to everyday users. Why was this content held to a different standard when it was raised by a reporter, and not when it was flagged through official Facebook channels by a normal account holder?

Asked about the gap between its response to a user on the platform versus a media inquiry, Meta defended its record on removing abusive material from its platform.

“While there are times we miss things, we work hard to enforce our rules, which is shown by the fact that just last quarter, we proactively found and removed 98 percent of child endangerment posts before they were ever reported to us,” it said.

After we reported the abusive pages, Facebook’s recommendation algorithm started serving up many more similar AI videos of coaches inappropriately touching, kissing, and groping young athletes in the feed of the account we used to flag it. The implication is dark: that Meta has the tech it needs to identify the disturbing clips, but instead of using it to crack down on the content, it’s using it to recommend more of the material to users who have interacted with it.

The accounts often publish several near-identical AI videos per day, with some videos accumulating huge numbers of views. One video served to us after Meta shared its statement showed more than 176,000 views just two days after it was posted.

“I really enjoyed that session. I feel fresh and positive now,” a girl decked in a pink leotard and matching socks, standing on one leg and holding the other in the air, tells the camera as a gray-haired trainer pats her genitals. Hash tags in the video’s caption include “#ballettok,” “#ballerina,” and “#balletmemes.”

It’s hard to imagine that some of the videos aren’t being served by Meta’s algorithms to actual young athletes, raising the risk that they’ll see the grooming and abuse behavior normalized as they navigate the possibility of real-world exploitation.

“I’m extremely concerned that children who are exposed to this content will internalize the message that if something similar is happening to them, they have to endure it because it is normalized in similar environments… they will be forced to further suppress their innate wisdom that this type of contact with an adult is not okay,” Shore told us. “Sport already does this to children by normalizing physical discomfort like training on injuries. Young athletes are taught to trust their coaches, follow instructions and accept physical contact as part of training. These images reinforce the dangerous idea that inappropriate touching or sexualized behavior is simply part of the coach-athlete relationship and athletes should accept it, tolerate it or even be grateful for the attention.”

Shore added that one of her “greatest concerns” is that real-world predators could model behavior based on the abuse material proliferating on Facebook.

“This AI-generated material acts a ‘how to’ manual for inappropriate behavior, particularly when abusive interactions are presented as ordinary coaching practices or expressions of care. It risks giving adults who are already inclined to exploit their authority examples of how to disguise abusive conduct as legitimate coaching, affection or playfulness,” she said. “We need to recognize that this material doesn’t exist in isolation. It circulates within a sporting culture where athletes have historically been conditioned to comply with authority, where boundaries have too often been blurred, and where abuse has frequently been minimized or excused.”

“This content is normalizing behaviors,” she added, “that safeguarding efforts have spent decades trying to challenge.”

As Futurism previously reported , Meta has also declined to remove AI-generated content depicting extreme physical child abuse . The company has elsewhere failed to catch hundreds of paid advertisements containing real and AI-generated child sexual abuse material, as Wired reported in September . Meta also faced backlash last year after Reuters reported on internal documents stating that Meta chatbots were allowed to “engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual.”

Women’s and youth sports are notorious hunting grounds for abusers. According to a global 2021 study by the World Players Association, 13 percent of child athletes are subject to some kind of sexual abuse during their time in sports. That figure is likely an undercount, as TIME noted at the time , given that sexual abuse often goes unreported.

In that context, the AI-generated Facebook clips of older men abusing their proximity to girls’ and women’s bodies to groom, sexualize, and exploit them is particularly appalling. That the athletes depicted in the videos are shown acting enthusiastic in the face of the predation is even worse, adding an air of normalization — or even romanticization — to the clearly exploitative encounters displayed in the AI-generated clips.

But instead of taking its responsibility to police its platform seriously, it seems like Meta is operating by two different standards: dismissing regular users who report disturbing material, while jumping into action when it senses the threat of negative attention.

Microsoft just filed a patent for an AI product that would be able to transform live video in real time to alter speakers’ words and faces.

The patent, as first flagged by patent-tracker Patentlyze , is described by its inventors as a “near real-time artificial intelligence (AI) enhancement of video or augmented reality (AR) presentations of live events.”

Using AI agents, the system would identify and alter or remove certain words, while editing a speaker’s face and mouth to match. The agents would rely on set parameters or user profiles to make the changes, and would also edit the video and audio just before and after a removed or replaced word to allow for “smooth transitions.”

In an era of media and the internet increasingly defined by AI-fueled deepfakes, disinformation, and information-muddling slop, the system described in this patent may represent a new world of filtering tools that subtly alter reality as it takes place, in this case on a highly-personalized level. Viewers, the patent suggests, could consume whatever live event they want to without hearing what they don’t want to hear.

The potential use cases floated in the patent vary. One possible application is real-time translation, with the system allowing for broadcasts and other live footage to be both heard and seen in a viewer’s preferred language.

The patent also posits that such a tool could be used to remove filler words like “um” or “ah” from live speech, or to erase stutters or speech impediments.

Other possible use cases, though, go much further. According to the patent, the system could be used to cut down on “personal words or phrases” like “coined terms,” as well as “colloquial terms” like the term “y’all” or the phrase “bite the bullet.” The patent also claims that the system could eliminate “mumbled words, mispronounced words, misused words, misspoken words, offensive words, insensitive words, or inappropriate words.” Replacement words, it adds, may come from an “internet search.”

In other words, live broadcasts may not be so live anymore after all.

Microsoft didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Dubbing has existed for ages, and video footage is edited all the time, both for normal and for insidious reasons. Automatically editing live videos in this way with the help of AI agents, however, could change how audiences fundamentally engage with live footage. As it stands, if people don’t like what they hear, they can simply turn something off; the system outlined by Microsoft describes an environment where people can instead adjust someone else’s speech to their personal taste. Language translation aside, does using a tool that eliminates errors, or erases words and phrases associated with a speaker’s local dialect, move us further into personalized bubbles? What’s so bad about hearing someone from the South say “y’all?”

To that end, the patent does mention that an event’s original live video and audio may be recorded and stored for the sake of “ground truth,” nodding to potential misuse and confusion that could arise from such a tool.

The kinds of live footage that could be transformed by the system include lectures, presentations, a range of television productions — awards ceremonies, game and cooking shows — and live sports, among several others.

OpenAI is looking to pave over its fundamentally fractured relationship with the public by arguing that data centers can “transform host communities” and bring “thousands of jobs,” per Axios , in widely disputed claims that conveniently gloss over the fact that those benefits rarely stick around once construction is complete.

Michigan is set to deploy a major new software system to prisons across the state, meant to classify incarcerated people based on “how dangerous they are.”

That’s according to Detroit channel Fox2 , which reports that the Michigan Department of Corrections is plowing ahead with an inmate categorization algorithm that will sort people into various housing levels.

In Michigan, incarcerated people are separated into five housing levels according to their security classification. In the past, screenings were performed by a committee of staff appointed by the Warden at each facility. Now, it seems the state wants to outsource that decision — or at least have it be heavily informed by — a non-profit AI and software company called Recidiviz.

Recidiviz began as a data organization project at Google, meant to “uncover how technology could standardize criminal justice data and improve the system nationwide.” Its AI-integrated software platform is said to perform features like identifying individuals eligible for state-offered programs, reclassification, or release, and coordinate access to resources like transitional housing and employment.

In a since-deleted press release , MDOC said the Recidiviz software will be used to “optimize placement of incarcerated individuals” starting with a pilot program in a number of men’s facilities beginning in December. The state agency notes that the tool is expected to “improve MDOC’s ability to more accurately predict incarcerated individuals’ risk of future violence by approximately 30 percent,” though how the state arrived at that vague figure is unclear.

In comments to Futurism , both MDOC and Recidiviz denied that the specific piece of software being workshopped for Michigan prisons — which they termed a “classification module” — uses AI to administer placement decisions.

“AI is never used in Recidiviz tools to make decisions about anyone’s security level or release,” a spokesperson for the company claimed.

That said, it’s hard to ignore the fact that AI features prominently on Recidiviz’s website and in its marketing material.

One explainer states that “the Recidiviz Corrections Platform uses data, automation, and AI to save staff time,” while an info-tab on the company’s “Intake” capabilities states that Recidiviz allows corrections officials to “administer AI-powered conversational assessments, letting residents respond at their own pace and in their preferred language while still capturing the essential data staff need.”

Yet another page on the company’s website specifically about AI use states that “AI offers a way to reduce repetitive work, surface important insights faster, and improve consistency across teams.” Further down, the company states that it uses AI for things like “generating code across our open-source platforms” and “matching people with jobs, services, or support based on their needs.”

In a separate statement, MDOC public information officer Jenni Riehle asserted that “while Recidiviz builds AI tools that support staff with tasks such as meeting transcription, AI is never used to make decisions about an individual’s security level or release.”

But without a thorough look under the module’s hood, questions remain around where exactly in its platform Recidiviz deploys AI — and there is much at stake in the state’s decision.

For incarcerated people, housing designations are extremely consequential, determining which programming and resources they’ll be eligible for, and what kind of population they’ll be housed with for the duration of their sentence.

As a ProPublica investigation into a similar risk-analysis software in Louisiana found, the kind of data being used to classify incarcerated people contained inherent racial and socioeconomic bias.

As a result, Louisiana’s carceral system has become even more cruel and harmful to those earnestly working toward rehabilitation. In one case reported by ProPublica , a blind and wheelchair bound 70-year-old was determined to be a “moderate risk” of reoffending despite having a clean disciplinary record — a classification which results in an automatic loss of eligibility for parole.

While Michigan’s system is geared toward housing assignments rather than parole decisions, it seems highly unlikely that software alone will solve the state’s ongoing corrections crisis — and if Louisiana’s embrace of techno-solutionism is any example, it could very well make matters far, far worse.

AI companies sure have a funny marketing strategy.

When they’re not too busy predicting how their own tech will destroy the world , they like to insist that AI is well on its way to — or already has — surpassed the cognitive ability of humans. They’re grabbing customers by the shoulders, looking them dead in the eye, and telling them that they’ve now been rendered inferior beings. They’ll be honored, they seem to believe, to be a stepping stone towards progress (or tortured for eternity by a vindictive superintelligence for trying to stop AI from being brought about, according to certain utterly delusional corners of Silicon Valley.)

And that brings us to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Speaking at a conference in Abu Dhabi this week, Altman, whose company is under fire right now for allegedly disrespecting the entire field of mathematics , stressed that people should remain in control of the future, not AI. That’s when he snuck in a little side claim: that AI has now eclipsed even the brightest scientists — hence why it’s more urgent than ever that we keep a handle on our own destiny.

At the start of this year, “AI was mostly not as smart as our smartest scientists. And now it’s mostly smarter than them,” Altman said at the conference, in conversation with the editor-in-chief of the UAE state-owned paper The National .

Altman and OpenAI have long banged on about the intelligence of its models with respect to human scholars. When it released GPT-5 last year, it touted it as having “PhD-levels” of intelligence, and was routinely mocked for that obviously not being the case. Altman has also frequently predicted that AI will surpass human intelligence by the end of the decade.

This year, the “PhD-level” claim actually appeared to come true, sort of. OpenAI announced that it found a solution to the Navier-Stokes equations as laid out in the famous Millennium Prize Problems, something no human mathematician had ever solved. That caused a blowup ( get it? ) because a mathematician accused OpenAI of unfairly using his research, fueling discussions about how OpenAI was treating the math community.

OpenAI then poured fuel on the tire — or should we say, threw tons of paper on it — by simultaneously releasing hundreds of studies documenting purported solutions to even more math problems. Prominent mathematicians were incensed at how the community was being treated as unpaid proofreaders for OpenAI’s mountain of output, while OpenAI got to glorify their model as already matching their human intellect.

For Altman to come out and say that AI is now smarter than scientists when he has a significant chunk of the scientific community gunning for him is, shall we say, a choice. It’s also a claim that needs proof. The math fiasco is a good example of why it remains dubious. While the solutions appear technically correct, the actual natural language of the AI proofs are borderline incomprehensible , and it will probably take researchers years to unpack them all. As such, their actual utility to the field remains questionable.

From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear.

In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated.

As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation.

“I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar .

Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months.

In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name.

In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies.

As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.”

Despite a visibly degrading job market and widespread anxiety around AI automation, empirical evidence definitively linking the two phenomena has been hard to come by. Until now, at least.

New reporting by the Financial Times details two new sources of data pointing to AI’s impact on the labor market.

First, there was a new analysis by US-based financial researcher Eric Basmajian, who recently wrote in a post on social media that “AI productivity gains are showing up” in jobs data — with the caveat that only about 15 percent of jobs seem to be impacted so far.

“The three heaviest AI adopters (information, professional services, finance) went from a 2.2 percent productivity trend to 5.0 percent since 2022,” Basmajian explained, pointing to incremental gains in workplace productivity coinciding with a high AI adoption rate.

The very next day after Basmajian’s post, what appears to be an internal Goldman Sachs report began circulating on social media. It warned that the “AI labor market impact” has been spreading beyond tech work — a field that has already been hit hard as generative AI becomes a common tool for writing software code.

The report shows a rising trend between an industry’s AI exposure and unemployment around non-tech professional sectors like finance, telecomms, technical services, and administration, seemingly reinforcing Basmajian’s assertion.

But while there does seem to be a positive trendline in at least some areas of the job market, the FT tacks on a veritable laundry list of disclaimers.

Perhaps most importantly, the metrics looking at “productivity” in these cases aren’t necessarily reflective of quality — meaning we’re not necessarily talking about skyrocketing productive output and revenue as a result of AI, but of lower headcount, which is a big difference.

The data is also specifically about the US, pointing to broader post-Pandemic economic woes rather than a global AI jobpocalypse. As the FT explains, the “link that was visible in the US between AI usage on the one hand, and productivity growth and falling employment on the other, is conspicuously absent elsewhere.”

Either way, it seems the AI doomers finally have something to write home about as far as the labor market is concerned — though anyone preparing their bunker for a hypothetical AI labor revolution is going to have to keep on waiting.

https://futurism.com/future-society/goog.markdown:
Schools across the country have long grown dependent on Google, from its eponymous search engine to services like Gmail and Chromebooks, the company’s cheap laptops that have become commonplace in classrooms.

But it’s a fraught relationship that’s now seriously being tested as teachers start to suspect that the AI use is wreaking havoc on the impressionable minds of their students. The tech has been shown to erode young people’s critical thinking skills , cause their testing skills to plummet , and — at the extreme end — drive them into isolation and AI psychosis .

Google is now putting on brass knuckles to keep its AI in schools, saying that it’ll be unwilling to support schools that move to block AI entirely. As the New York Times reports , the tech giant is revoking access to Google Search, the most important gateway to information on the open web, for any schools looking to restrict AI.

It’s a spiteful move that could greatly deteriorate the company’s already tenuous relationship with educators. Put differently, Google is holding schools hostage by withholding its number one bargaining chip from any institution willing to say no to AI. The decision could force teachers’ and administrators’ hands as they watch AI destroy a generation of students .

Google has plastered “AI Overviews” on top of its search engine, entangling the two products. But the service’s answers are its frequently wrong, turning the very top of company’s index of the internet into a massive minefield of misinformation .

“Search and AI are deeply integrated,” Google VP of education Chris Phillips told the NYT . If a school bans AI, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

The company has been advertising its Gemini AI chatbot to schools as a way to help teachers and provide personalized tutors to students. It forced the AI features on classrooms earlier this year by making them the default, triggering a major outcry among educators.

The news comes as state regulators continue to ponder how to set rules for the use of AI in public education and by minors as a whole. Several school districts across New York and California have restricted some of these features on school devices, with the hopes of regaining access to traditional search without AI Overviews.

But that option no longer appears to be on the table as Google looks to force AI into classrooms. The company announced this week that schools can either choose to have search with AI Overviews turned on — or a student-oriented version of its Gemini chatbot, called Guided Learning.

Those two options are unlikely to get a glowing reception from frustrated educators looking to protect children from the many harmful effects of AI.

https://futurism.com/future-society/inve.markdown:
For years now, some of the biggest players in the AI space have been investing in smaller startups — which in turn use the same exact money to purchase services from the same large companies.

Investors have watched this circular financing with quiet but growing trepidation. After all, as the Wall Street Journal points out , if the AI bubble were to pop, the consequences could be dire. Now, with fears over a sudden collapse are as palpable as ever, such a “tangled web of AI bets,” as the newspaper puts it, could spell disaster.

The signs aren’t exactly hard to identify. Just last week, Google’s parent company Alphabet experienced the biggest drop in its market value in its history, wiping out well over half a trillion dollars in value .

The accompanying crash likely didn’t just send jitters across tech markets. Since the AI industry is effectively propping up the entire US economy, its failure could have far-reaching consequences to a public that’s increasingly skeptical of its offerings .

Since most of these companies’ fates are inextricably linked by circular financing, a major economic downturn or weakening demand could have cascading repercussions, especially considering much of the sector’s financing is based on debt.

Beyond the tech industry’s very bad week, data center operators aren’t looking much better. Nvidia customer CoreWave, which analysts have dubbed the “ AI trade’s canary in the coal mine ,” has also seen its shares decline over months, raising plenty of flags .

Despite the widespread unease, enormous data center expansion efforts are in full swing, major bipartisan backlash notwithstanding. It’s an unprecedented all-in that could jeopardize the entire economy if it were to collapse.

Even beyond the US, the circular financing is starting to worry investors in Asia. The Bank of Korea recently warned of a “semiconductor version of Dutch disease,” an economic concept describing a booming sector that overtakes all other tradable market segments.

Yet the country is doubling down, with president Lee Jae Myung pledging today to “boldly invest in AI and future growth engines,” effectively doubling AI and chip spending for next year.

Only time will tell whether that’ll be the right move as more and more investors get cold feet.

https://futurism.com/robots-and-machines.markdown:
AI robots couldn’t let us keep our vanity to ourselves. They’re now hitting the gym, too — but the reps they’re getting in aren’t of the weightlifting kind.

Enter Neura, a buzzy robotics startup in Metzingen, Germany, that is positioning itself at the forefront of embodied AI by training these advanced systems to inhabit and navigate the real world.

According to a new piece from the New York Times , the heart of its operations is its secretive “robogym” facility in Munich, where up to one hundred humanoids from companies around the world constantly practice and perform tasks — from chores to factory work — so they can get better at them.

The NYT described the scene, in the first time a journalist has been given access to the facility: “The robots picked up car parts and placed them into containers, stacked boxes and carried out other tasks, mimicking the movements of human trainers who guided them remotely. One robot practiced tightening its grip on a glass, learning how to respond when water is added.”

Large language models can draw on existing data, from internet posts to books, to “learn” about the world. But the equivalent corpus of data doesn’t exist for the physical world, so it has to be created and collected .

Neura founder David Reger likened it to learning to swim, telling the NYT that you can’t simply watch videos; you have to get in the water.

Having recently raised up to $1.4 billion from the likes of Nvidia and Amazon in a June funding round, Neura is gunning to become something like the Gold’s Gym of the robo world. By the end of next year, per the NYT , it plans to operate five gyms across the globe. It already has one in Hangzhou, China, one of the country’s major tech hubs.

It’s a leader in the West, but it’s playing catch up with Chinese competitors, who altogether already run more than 90 humanoid data collection centers, according to data from the consulting firm Interact Analysis, while Europe only has ten.

Currently, most robots used in factories are specialized for specific tasks. Humanoid robots aim to be versatile like a real employee, but are harder to pull off. There’s still huge questions over their, but the idea seems to making some headway, with BMW preparing to trial robots from the Swiss company Hexagon Robotics on the factory floor. Japan Airlines is also experimenting with robot baggage handlers at Tokyo’s Haneda airport, who presumably have had plenty of time to hit the gym.
